extracted.intended_audience: scientific journal reviewers and editors (peer reviewers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for individuals who evaluate manuscripts for scientific journals, covering reviewer responsibilities to authors, editors, and readers; reviewer selection; ethical duties; and norms around anonymity and recognition. Intended to guide how to perform and manage peer review appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide written, unbiased, constructive feedback in a timely manner
rubrics_metrics.description: Providing written, unbiased, constructive feedback in a timely manner on the scholarly merits and the scientific value of the work, together with the documented basis for the reviewer’s opinion
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers should explain and support their judgments clearly so editors and authors can understand the basis of comments. Timeliness is emphasized throughout the section; reviewers should act promptly and adhere to deadlines (see timeliness entry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess clarity, composition, accuracy, originality, and interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicating whether the writing is clear, concise, and relevant and rating the work’s composition, scientific accuracy, originality, and interest to the journal’s readers
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers should evaluate both scientific substance and presentation; comment on writing and organization as well as on novelty and relevance to the journal’s audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid personal comments or criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoiding personal comments or criticism
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All anonymous comments should be courteous and capable of withstanding public scrutiny; personal or ad hominem criticism is explicitly listed as an example of impropriety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain confidentiality of the review process
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintaining the confidentiality of the review process: not sharing, discussing with third parties, or disclosing information from the reviewed paper
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material under review is privileged communication; reviewers should not retain copies of manuscripts or use knowledge for purposes unrelated to review. If unsure about enlisting help, ask the editor. Breaching confidentiality (sharing, discussing, or using information) is listed as reviewer impropriety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notify editor if unable to review and suggest alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Notifying the editor immediately if unable to review in a timely manner and, if able, providing the names of alternative reviewers
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors rely on reviewers to meet timelines; prompt notification helps avoid delays. Reviewer selection processes may ask reviewers to disclose availability up front.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose and manage conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Alerting the editor about any potential personal, financial or perceived conflict of interest and declining to review when a conflict exists
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers should either decline or disclose conflicts and ask the editor how best to address them. Some journals require signed disclosure forms. Failure to disclose a conflict that would have excluded a reviewer is cited as impropriety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow the editor’s instructions on scope, content, and quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Complying with the editor’s written instructions on the journal’s expectations for the scope, content, and quality of the review
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors may request specific types of evaluation or separate confidential comments for editors; reviewers should adhere to requested formats and rating scales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide thoughtful, fair, constructive, and informative critique
rubrics_metrics.description: Providing a thoughtful, fair, constructive, and informative critique of the submitted work, which may include supplementary material provided to the journal by the author
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique may include suggested improvements, methodological advice, and, if requested, a recommendation (accept/revise/reject) using whatever rating scale the editor deems useful. The purpose is to help authors resolve weaknesses, not to display the reviewer’s ability to find flaws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess scientific merit, originality, and scope; recommend improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: Determining scientific merit, originality, and scope of the work; indicating ways to improve it; and, if requested, recommending acceptance or rejection
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers should identify strengths and weaknesses and provide concrete suggestions for improvement. In cases of controversy an additional review or editor evaluation may be solicited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Note ethical concerns (human/animal subjects, redundancy, plagiarism, fabricated data)
rubrics_metrics.description: Noting any ethical concerns, such as any violation of accepted norms of ethical treatment of animal or human subjects or substantial similarity between the reviewed manuscript and any published paper or any manuscript concurrently submitted to another journal that may be known to the reviewer
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When suspecting ethical problems (duplicate publication, plagiarism, fabricated data, undisclosed conflicts), reviewers should immediately alert the editor and may consult COPE flowcharts and other resources cited in the section.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refrain from direct author contact
rubrics_metrics.description: Refraining from direct author contact
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All communications about the manuscript should go through the editor to preserve confidentiality and avoid conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure methods and analysis allow judgment and replication
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensuring that the methods and analysis are adequately detailed to allow the reader to judge the scientific merit of the study design and be able to replicate the study
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers should flag inadequate methods, missing details, or analyses that prevent reproducibility; this is a responsibility toward readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure the article cites all relevant prior work
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensuring that the article cites all relevant work by other scientists
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers should point out missing citations, request acknowledgment of prior relevant work, and ensure proper attribution; failure to cite relevant work can be an ethical concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select reviewers with appropriate expertise and avoid overburdening
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should choose reviewers whose expertise most closely matches the manuscript’s topic and consider the number of manuscripts sent to a reviewer so as not to overburden any one expert
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors are encouraged to consider diversity when selecting reviewers. Bias screening (e.g., excluding reviewers from the same department/institution) can be built into submission systems or policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bias screening in reviewer selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer selection process should address potential bias by excluding reviewers from the same department or institution as the author(s) and by asking reviewers to disclose any potential conflict of interest
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This screening can be incorporated into online forms, invitation emails, or posted policies. Reviewers should decline if they have personal or professional connections that could be perceived as conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive critique practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer comments should acknowledge the positive aspects of the material under review, identify negative aspects constructively, and indicate the improvements needed
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments should be supported by explanation and citations for prior work. The reviewer should respect the author's intellectual independence. Some journals request separate confidential comments to editors that may be more candid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competence: accept only assignments within expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers who realize that their expertise on the subject of the manuscript is limited have a responsibility to make their degree of competence clear to the editor and should accept an assignment only if they have adequate expertise to provide an authoritative assessment
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reviewer lacking requisite expertise risks incorrect recommendations and should decline the review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartiality and integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer comments and conclusions should be based on an objective and impartial consideration of the facts, exclusive of personal or professional bias
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments should be based on scientific merit, originality, quality of writing, and relevance to the journal without regard to authors' race, sex, religion, citizenship, etc. Reviewers must avoid using privileged information for personal or professional advantage and avoid even the appearance of such behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of conflict of interest procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: If reviewers have any interest that might interfere with an objective review, they should either decline the role of reviewer or disclose their conflict of interest to the editor and ask how best to address it
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some journals require reviewers to sign disclosure forms similar to authors'; the review system should be designed to minimize actual or perceived bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness and responsiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers are responsible for acting promptly, adhering to the instructions for completing a review, and submitting it in a timely manner
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If unable to meet the deadline, the reviewer should promptly decline or inquire about accommodations. Unreasonable delay is listed as reviewer impropriety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of reviewer impropriety (prohibited behaviors)
rubrics_metrics.description: List of improper behaviors: misrepresenting facts in a review; unreasonably delaying the review process; unfairly criticizing a competitor’s work; breaching confidentiality; proposing changes that merely support the reviewer’s own work; making use of confidential information for personal gain; using ideas or text from a manuscript under review; including personal or ad hominem criticism; failing to disclose a conflict of interest that would have excluded the reviewer
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These examples serve as explicit anti-patterns and misconduct indicators; editors should act if such behavior is suspected, and reviewers must avoid these actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymity vs open peer review norms and tradeoffs
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion of single-masked (single-blind), double-masked (double-anonymous), and fully open peer review systems, noting arguments for and against each model
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most editors consider reviewer anonymity a norm. Potential problems include subjectivity, bias, misuse of ideas, and decreased accountability; open review may reduce anonymous abuses but can cause animosity or reduced criticalness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewarding and recognizing reviewers appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals may publicly thank reviewers (e.g., published list) but should obtain permission before disclosing reviewer names; journals may offer CME credits; recognition services like Publons or ORCID Reviewer Recognition can be used
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognition should respect confidentiality and regulations such as GDPR; reviewer recognition programs require collaboration between reviewers and journals.
